newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA MAY BE HEADING FOR RECESSION - ECONOMIST.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA MAY BE HEADING FOR RECESSION - ECONOMIST.

text.p: South African economic growth has stopped and the country will enter a recession soon, E.W. Balderson economist Mike Schussler said on Monday.

Citing negative growth in container imports, lower commodity prices and struggling exports, Schussler said in a research note he believed GDP growth would be negative in the second and third quarters of this year.
South Africa's economy contracted by 0.8 percent on an annualised basis in the first quarter of 1997 from the fourth quarter of 1996.
"We do not see any growth before the fourth quarter any more and the year will probably average in the negative," he said.
"Growth has not slowed it has stopped and South Africa will officially enter the recession soon."
Schussler said that for the first time since the end of 1992, average container imports on a three-month moving average basis had turned negative for a full three months.
Container imports had shown negative growth of 6.8 percent for the first five months of this year, he said.
He said container imports were a coincidental indicator of gross domestic product (GDP) and had shown a close correlation since 1981.
"What the relationship currently shows is that GDP growth is starting to turn negative."

He also noted that revised total volume figures to the end of May also revealed that, despite the increase in crude oil imports, four of the last five months total import figures were showing strong negative growth.

"Current indications are that containers are slowing even Schussler said that in the face of weaker commodity prices and capacity constraints in the agriculture sector, exports appeared to be struggling to lead any recovery.
"Exports, which showed much promise in December, might still be growing, but have slackened off quite a bit in recent months."
He said airport outgoing freight was still growing at 20 percent in June, but that this was down from 53 percent in January and 101 percent in July 1996.
"This may be the time for interest rate cuts, sooner and faster in the next few quarters than most people have anticipated," he said.
"...That cuts will be needed soon are evident in the speed of the slowdown of imports. The speed of the drop is faster than any other since 1985 on a three-month moving average basis," he said.
Bank rate, currently 17 percent, was last changed in November last year, when it was increased by one percentage point.
